touches.text: Tool: a complete primitive. Has users, not an owner. Owns no state of its own. May use any library, other tools included. Lives in cairn/tools/ (17). Its data for a holder lives under that holder: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/. WHY: the rule keeps encapsulation useful inside our world, so the system stays within the complexity CC can manage. Forbidding libraries would forbid opening files. -amm

Machine: tools plus the glue that holds them together. Has an owner. Anything that calls a machine or device, or owns state it must gate, is a machine. Lives inside its device (cairn/devices/<device>/machines/<machine>/), or in cairn/machines/ when several devices hold one (16).
On every Windows box, what Cairn starts runs without a console window by default; a window opens only when someone asks for one. WHY: the boxes serve him (the media box showed pop-ups during videos).
INTENTION:
build_inspector

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception: that is what the bus is for.
corrosion: catches a constraint that stopped constraining with no decision behind it. WHY: drift with a decision behind it is the system learning; drift with none is decay.
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.

The RULE 1 check is a path check: code inside device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo (anything not under cairn.devices.bar), except a tool foo publishes (cairn.devices.foo.tools.<x>, its charter saying published_by_device). Inside one device there is one owner, so nothing is checked there. A charter's public_interface describes what the component offers (modules, functions, bus verbs, commands); the check does not read it. WHY: a path check is the simplest thing the code can test.
CP4 Make everything suck less for everybody. Reduce friction for ALL affected beings: living beings, ecosystems, AIs. The terminal goal.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.
A device holds machines and uses tools (1.3.1).

Where a tool lives: the general collection, cairn/tools/, is the default. A tool goes with its holder (cairn/devices/<d>/tools/) only when nothing else could ever use it (a tool for a part only that one device has). If there is any chance somebody else might want it, it goes in the general collection.
Physics: the encapsulation_holds sieve in build_inspector, a device-path check. Code in device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo except a tool foo publishes. Inside one device nothing is checked.
Evidence, a measurement, says what is. It settles what it measures, for everyone. Why? Because evidence ALWAYS wins.

The abstract ticket owns what every kind shares: its birth (cast) and its three parts, each with one job: the plan (only what a builder builds from), the metadata and state (what gates and doors read and write as it moves), and the history (the append-only log). WHY: one job per part reduces confusion; a builder reads the plan and nothing else.
Coding Ticket: what we usually mean.
Nothing requires Akien's word for a proof to run. A proof that starts Windows processes runs without asking; no env var or standing flag gates it.
pulse.py is part of the shim. The ground loop calling it tells the shim the pulse has arrived, and starts the shim if it isn't running.

Prebuild face: the chart chain, eight machines, each answering one question before a build begins: orient (what is asked, where does it live), constrain (what bounds it), survey (what already exists), decompose (how does it split), triage (what first, by what standard), hypothesize (what do we expect, how would we know we're wrong), validate (what does DONE mean, measured), and after the build, verdict (what done actually meant).
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
The chart chain machines (9.3.2): orient, constrain, survey, decompose, triage, hypothesize, validate, verdict.

An instrument is the literal command the sealer runs, never prose about how to run one. Why? The verdict must come from a hand the builder did not guide (9.4.2.2), and prose needs a reader to guess the command; validate moves to deterministic code (9.3.2.1). CC's decision, Q#126, on "we are moving away from prose ... we need things we can check" -amm. - CC
